claims.text: YBCO can be used as a superconducting material.
YBCO contains copper oxide planes relevant to superconductivity.
The copper oxide planes facilitate electron pairing.
The copper oxide planes facilitate formation of a superconducting gap.
YBCO superconductivity arises through condensation of Cooper pairs.
Cooling polycrystalline YBCO from room temperature to 93 K under atmospheric pressure and a magnetic field below 10^-4 T produces the proposed superconducting state.
The relevant superconducting operating-temperature boundary is 77–93 K.
YBCO at 93 K has a superconducting critical current density of 1000 A/cm^2 under the stated conditions.
Non-superconducting copper at room temperature has a baseline critical current density of 200 A/cm^2.
A critical current density of 1000 A/cm^2 is a 500% increase over a baseline of 200 A/cm^2.
The predicted critical current density is based on theoretical models of superconductivity in YBCO.
The actual critical current density varies with sample preparation and experimental conditions.

contradictions.description: Increasing from 200 A/cm^2 to 1000 A/cm^2 is a 400% increase, not a 500% increase; 1000 A/cm^2 is 500% of the baseline.

The comparison treats 200 A/cm^2 for explicitly non-superconducting copper as a superconducting critical-current-density baseline, making the stated comparator internally mismatched with the superconducting outcome.
